ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Gastroenterology Consultation — Natsume Sōseki — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Gastroenterology consultation with upper endoscopy and biopsy, diagnosis of gastric ulcer, and start of vonoprazan and iron

text.paragraph: Suspected bleeding peptic ulcer in a 43-year-old novelist with three weeks of epigastric pain, two black, tarry stools ten days ago, and iron-deficiency anemia, after occasional ibuprofen. Please perform upper endoscopy with biopsy, exclude gastric cancer, test for Helicobacter pylori, and advise on treatment and follow-up. [S]

Urgency: Urgent, within three days. He is stable today with no further black stools; Glasgow-Blatchford score 4 (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL and the history of melena). He has been told to call 119 or go to the emergency department at once for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, fainting, or severe pain. No acid suppression has been started, so that the biopsies are not affected, unless bleeding recurs. [S]

list.item: What is the source of the bleeding, and is this a peptic ulcer?
Can gastric cancer be excluded, and what biopsies are needed?
Does he have Helicobacter pylori, and which eradication regimen do you advise given clarithromycin resistance in Japan?
Can he be treated at home, and what acid suppression and follow-up endoscopy do you advise?
Does the iron-deficiency anemia need colonoscopy as well?
Does he need surveillance for gastric cancer after treatment?

text.paragraph: Mr. Natsume, a 43-year-old novelist, is seen at the request of Dr. Lindqvist-Mori three days after his first visit. He describes three weeks of gnawing upper abdominal pain before meals and at night, relieved by food, and two black, tarry stools about two weeks ago, with none since. He had taken ibuprofen for headaches a few times a month and stopped it at his first visit. He has not vomited blood, lost weight, or had trouble swallowing. He does not smoke and rarely drinks. He has never had an endoscopy. He is worried about stomach cancer and wants to keep writing his newspaper serial. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Natsume Sōseki, whose name was Natsume Kinnosuke, was born on the 5th day of the 1st month of Keiō 3 in the Japanese calendar (9 February 1867) in Ushigome Babashita-Yokomachi in Edo, now Kikui-chō in Shinjuku, Tokyo, the son of a town headman. [D]
At the age of one he was adopted into the Shiobara family; his adoptive parents divorced when he was nine, and he was returned to his birth family. [D]

After graduating from the English department of the Imperial University in 1893 he taught at Matsuyama Middle School and at the Fifth Higher School in Kumamoto, and married Nakane Kyōko, eldest daughter of Nakane Shigeichi, chief secretary of the House of Peers, after taking up the Kumamoto post. [D]
In 1900, at 33, he was sent by the Ministry of Education to Britain to study English for two years, and he returned to Japan in 1903. [D]
During his stay in Britain he soon felt at odds with the study of English literature and fell into a state of severe nervous distress, which continued after his return. [D]

The city of Shinjuku calls the London illness shinkei suijaku (nervous breakdown, neurasthenia), and the Sōseki museum calls it nervous depression; both are labels of the period or translations of it, not modern diagnoses. [R]

In 1907, at 40, he gave up all his teaching posts and joined the Asahi Shimbun as a staff writer, and about then moved to Waseda-Minami-chō; Sanshirō, Sorekara and Mon were serialized in the newspaper. He had made his name with I Am a Cat (1905 to 1906) and later wrote Kokoro (1914). [D]
From about May 1910, while writing Mon, he suffered from stomach illness, a gastric ulcer. [D]

code.displayName: Relevant Diagnostic Tests and/or Laboratory Data

list.item: Gastric ulcer with recent bleeding (K25.4). The source is a 15 mm gastric ulcer at the angulus with a clean base, which carries a low risk of rebleeding and needs no endoscopic treatment. The likely causes are Helicobacter pylori and the ibuprofen. With a stable hemoglobin and normal pulse and blood pressure, he can be treated at home. The ulcer looks benign, but a gastric ulcer must be biopsied and followed to healing because an early gastric cancer can look like one. [S]

Helicobacter pylori infection (B96.81). The rapid urease test is positive. Clarithromycin resistance is common in Japan, so the regimen should follow the PCR result: vonoprazan, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 7 days if the strain is susceptible, or vonoprazan 20 mg twice daily with amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 14 days if it is resistant. Bismuth quadruple therapy, preferred elsewhere when susceptibility is unknown, is not available for this use in Japan. [S]

Iron-deficiency anemia (D50.0). Explained by the bleeding ulcer. In an adult man with iron-deficiency anemia a colonoscopy is usually advised too, but with an upper source found and no bowel symptoms it can wait to see whether the anemia corrects once the ulcer heals; if it does not, colonoscopy is needed. [S]

Gastric cancer risk. The open-type atrophy at endoscopy suggests long-standing infection; the mapping biopsies will stage atrophy and intestinal metaplasia. Eradication lowers the risk of gastric cancer but does not remove it when atrophy is extensive, so surveillance endoscopy is likely to be needed. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Lindqvist-Mori's intake note and results: hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL with MCV 76 fL and ferritin 8 ng/mL; urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL; Glasgow-Blatchford score 4. Hemoglobin this morning 11.0 g/dL. Upper endoscopy this morning under light sedation: normal esophagus; a 15 mm ulcer on the lesser curvature at the angulus with a clean white base and no visible vessel or adherent clot (Forrest III), regular margins and smooth converging folds; open-type atrophy (Kimura-Takemoto O-1) with antral nodularity; no blood in the stomach; normal duodenum. Six biopsies were taken from the ulcer margin, five mapping biopsies (updated Sydney protocol) for histology, and a biopsy for clarithromycin-resistance PCR. Rapid urease test positive. [S]

list.item: Start vonoprazan 20 mg each morning now, after the biopsies, and continue for eight weeks for a gastric ulcer. [S]
No NSAIDs, including aspirin and combination cold remedies; acetaminophen for pain; no smoking and little alcohol. [S]

Eradication at the two-week visit, chosen by the clarithromycin-resistance PCR: vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy for 14 days if resistant, or vonoprazan triple therapy with clarithromycin for 7 days if susceptible. [S]
Confirm eradication with a 13C urea breath test at least four weeks after the antibiotics and at least two weeks after stopping vonoprazan. [S]
Repeat endoscopy at about ten weeks to confirm healing and to biopsy the scar. [S]
Oral iron from today; colonoscopy only if the anemia does not correct after the ulcer has healed. [S]
Endoscopic surveillance after eradication if the biopsies confirm atrophy or intestinal metaplasia: yearly is usual practice in Japan for moderate or extensive atrophy. [S]
Call 119 or go to the emergency department for black, tarry stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, fainting, or sudden severe pain. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Lindqvist-Mori the same morning; she continues the prescribing, the iron and the follow-up. The endoscopy pictures were shown to Mr. Natsume, who asked whether it was cancer; he was told that the ulcer looks benign and that the biopsies would answer the question in about two weeks. [S]
Follow-up: Repeat endoscopy with Dr. Abrahamsen-Ito at about ten weeks, combined with the urea breath test; then yearly surveillance endoscopy if the histology confirms atrophy. [S]
